claim: Self-generated touch feels less intense than identical externally generated touch.
source: Self-generated touch feels less intense and less ticklish than identical externally generated touch.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Self-generated touch feels less ticklish than identical externally generated touch.
source: Self-generated touch feels less intense and less ticklish than identical externally generated touch.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Somatosensory attenuation occurs because the brain predicts the tactile consequences of self-generated movements.
source: This somatosensory attenuation occurs because the brain predicts the tactile consequences of our self-generated movements.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by the internal model framework cited in the introduction.

claim: Tactile predictions need to be time-locked to the movement to produce attenuation.
source: To produce attenuation, the tactile predictions need to be time-locked to the movement, but how the brain maintains this temporal tuning remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a known requirement, with the mechanism being the research question.

claim: People can rapidly unlearn to attenuate touch immediately after their movement after repeated exposure to a systematic delay.
source: Using a bimanual self-touch paradigm, we demonstrate that people can rapidly unlearn to attenuate touch immediately after their movement and learn to attenuate delayed touch instead, after repeated exposure to a systematic delay between the movement and the resulting touch.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: People can learn to attenuate delayed touch after repeated exposure to a systematic delay between movement and touch.
source: Using a bimanual self-touch paradigm, we demonstrate that people can rapidly unlearn to attenuate touch immediately after their movement and learn to attenuate delayed touch instead, after repeated exposure to a systematic delay between the movement and the resulting touch.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: The magnitudes of the unlearning and learning effects are correlated.
source: The magnitudes of the unlearning and learning effects are correlated and dependent on the number of trials that participants have been exposed to.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by correlation analysis in the results section.

claim: The magnitudes of the unlearning and learning effects are dependent on the number of trials that participants have been exposed to.
source: The magnitudes of the unlearning and learning effects are correlated and dependent on the number of trials that participants have been exposed to.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the additional experiment testing different numbers of exposure trials.

claim: Delayed touches feel less ticklish after exposure to systematic delay.
source: We further show that delayed touches feel less ticklish and non-delayed touches more ticklish after exposure to the systematic delay.
evidence: This is a finding from the tickling experiment reported in the results.

claim: Non-delayed touches feel more ticklish after exposure to systematic delay.
source: We further show that delayed touches feel less ticklish and non-delayed touches more ticklish after exposure to the systematic delay.
evidence: This is a finding from the tickling experiment reported in the results.

claim: The attenuation of self-generated touch is adaptive.
source: These findings demonstrate that the attenuation of self-generated touch is adaptive.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing learning and unlearning.

claim: The brain uses internal models to anticipate the sensory consequences of voluntary movements based on efference copy.
source: It is theorized that the brain uses internal models to anticipate the sensory consequences of voluntary movements on the basis of a copy of the motor command (efference copy) (Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001; Bays and Wolpert, 2007; Franklin and Wolpert, 2011; Blakemore et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sensory predictions are used to achieve efficient online motor control.
source: These sensory predictions are used to achieve efficient online motor control, to ensure movement stability and to reduce uncertainty, as the actual sensory feedback is delayed due to sensory transduction times (Kawato, 1999; Davidson and Wolpert, 2005; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to the motor control literature.

claim: Sensory predictions are used to ensure movement stability.
source: These sensory predictions are used to achieve efficient online motor control, to ensure movement stability and to reduce uncertainty, as the actual sensory feedback is delayed due to sensory transduction times (Kawato, 1999; Davidson and Wolpert, 2005; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to the motor control literature.

claim: Sensory predictions are used to reduce uncertainty.
source: These sensory predictions are used to achieve efficient online motor control, to ensure movement stability and to reduce uncertainty, as the actual sensory feedback is delayed due to sensory transduction times (Kawato, 1999; Davidson and Wolpert, 2005; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to the motor control literature.

claim: Actual sensory feedback is delayed due to sensory transduction times.
source: These sensory predictions are used to achieve efficient online motor control, to ensure movement stability and to reduce uncertainty, as the actual sensory feedback is delayed due to sensory transduction times (Kawato, 1999; Davidson and Wolpert, 2005; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008).
evidence: This is a known physiological fact cited from the literature.

claim: Predictions of internal models are used for attenuating the perception of self-produced input.
source: In addition, the predictions of the internal models are also used for attenuating the perception of self-produced input, thereby increasing the salience of unpredicted external signals and facilitating the perceptual distinction between the self and the environment (Blakemore et al., 2000a; Bays and Wolpert, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: Attenuation of self-produced input increases the salience of unpredicted external signals.
source: In addition, the predictions of the internal models are also used for attenuating the perception of self-produced input, thereby increasing the salience of unpredicted external signals and facilitating the perceptual distinction between the self and the environment (Blakemore et al., 2000a; Bays and Wolpert, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of sensory attenuation, supported by citations.

claim: Attenuation of self-produced input facilitates the perceptual distinction between the self and the environment.
source: In addition, the predictions of the internal models are also used for attenuating the perception of self-produced input, thereby increasing the salience of unpredicted external signals and facilitating the perceptual distinction between the self and the environment (Blakemore et al., 2000a; Bays and Wolpert, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of sensory attenuation, supported by citations.

claim: When one actively touches one's left hand with one's right, the touch feels less intense than identical touches applied by another person or a machine.
source: For example, when one actively touches one's left hand with one's right (self-touch), the touch feels less intense than identical touches applied to the left hand by another person or a machine (Blakemore et al., 2000a; Shergill et al., 2003; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an established finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Self-induced touch has been predicted by the internal model.
source: This is because the self-induced touch has been predicted by the internal model.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the internal model theory.

claim: Predictions of internal models are useful only if the models constitute accurate representations of the body and current environmental dynamics.
source: Importantly, the predictions of the internal models are useful only if the models constitute accurate representations of the body and the current environmental dynamics (Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Shadmehr et al., 2010; Wolpert et al., 1998; Miall, 2002; Haith and Krakauer, 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about internal models, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Biased predictions would be detrimental to motor performance.
source: Biased predictions would not only be detrimental to motor performance but also prevent one from distinguishing the sensory feedback of one's own movements from that produced by external causes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the internal model theory.

claim: Biased predictions would prevent one from distinguishing the sensory feedback of one's own movements from that produced by external causes.
source: Biased predictions would not only be detrimental to motor performance but also prevent one from distinguishing the sensory feedback of one's own movements from that produced by external causes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the internal model theory.

claim: Predictions of internal models are temporally locked to the given movement.
source: A good illustration of this sharp tuning of the internal models is that their predictions are temporally locked to the given movement (Figure 1a, left): for example, during self-touch, tactile feedback is expected at the time of contact between the hands, and touch that is artificially delayed (even by only 100 ms) shows reduced attenuation and is attributed to external causes rather than the self (Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: During self-touch, tactile feedback is expected at the time of contact between the hands.
source: A good illustration of this sharp tuning of the internal models is that their predictions are temporally locked to the given movement (Figure 1a, left): for example, during self-touch, tactile feedback is expected at the time of contact between the hands, and touch that is artificially delayed (even by only 100 ms) shows reduced attenuation and is attributed to external causes rather than the self (Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an example of temporal locking, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Touch that is artificially delayed by 100 ms shows reduced attenuation.
source: A good illustration of this sharp tuning of the internal models is that their predictions are temporally locked to the given movement (Figure 1a, left): for example, during self-touch, tactile feedback is expected at the time of contact between the hands, and touch that is artificially delayed (even by only 100 ms) shows reduced attenuation and is attributed to external causes rather than the self (Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an established finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Touch that is artificially delayed by 100 ms is attributed to external causes rather than the self.
source: A good illustration of this sharp tuning of the internal models is that their predictions are temporally locked to the given movement (Figure 1a, left): for example, during self-touch, tactile feedback is expected at the time of contact between the hands, and touch that is artificially delayed (even by only 100 ms) shows reduced attenuation and is attributed to external causes rather than the self (Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an established finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: When participants were exposed to a 0 ms delay, attenuation was observed only for the immediate test tap.
source: As expected from previous studies (Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999), when participants were exposed to a 0 ms delay, attenuation was observed only for the immediate test tap (paired t-test between [exposure delay = 0 ms, test delay = 0 ms] and baseline, t(29) = −4.65, p<0.001, CI95 = [−0.195,–0.076], BF10 = 369) and not for the delayed touch (paired Wilcoxon test between [0 ms, 100 ms] and baseline, n = 30, V = 226, p=0.903, CI95 = [−0.061, 0.056]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by statistical analysis and consistent with previous literature.

claim: When participants were exposed to a 0 ms delay, attenuation was not observed for the delayed touch.
source: As expected from previous studies (Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999), when participants were exposed to a 0 ms delay, attenuation was observed only for the immediate test tap (paired t-test between [exposure delay = 0 ms, test delay = 0 ms] and baseline, t(29) = −4.65, p<0.001, CI95 = [−0.195,–0.076], BF10 = 369) and not for the delayed touch (paired Wilcoxon test between [0 ms, 100 ms] and baseline, n = 30, V = 226, p=0.903, CI95 = [−0.061, 0.056]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by statistical analysis.

claim: After exposure to 0 ms delay, the immediate tap felt significantly less intense than the delayed one.
source: In line with this pattern, the immediate tap felt significantly less intense than the delayed one (paired Wilcoxon test between [0 ms, 0 ms] and [0 ms, 100 ms], n = 30, V = 18, p<0.001, CI95 = [−0.183,–0.09]).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by statistical analysis.

claim: After exposure to a 100 ms delay, the attenuation of the immediate tap significantly decreased.
source: Importantly however, the pattern of results reversed after exposure to a 100 ms delay: the attenuation of the immediate tap significantly decreased (paired t-test between [100 ms, 0 ms] and [0 ms, 0 ms], t(29) = 2.73, p=0.011, CI95 = [0.018, 0.128], BF10 = 4.241).
evidence: This is a key finding from the study supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The decrease in attenuation of immediate touch indicates that participants unlearned to predict touch at the time of contact.
source: This decrease in attenuation of immediate touch (Figure 2c) indicates that participants unlearned to predict touch at the time of contact.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 2c.

claim: After exposure to 100 ms delay, the attenuation of the delayed tap significantly increased.
source: In contrast, the attenuation of the delayed tap significantly increased (paired t-test between [100 ms, 100 ms] and [0 ms, 100 ms], t(29) = −3.29, p=0.003, CI95 = [−0.142,–0.033], BF10 = 14.311).
evidence: This is a key finding from the study supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The shift in attenuation of the delayed touch indicates that participants learned to predict the touch at the delay to which they were exposed.
source: This shift in attenuation of the delayed touch (Figure 2d) indicates that participants learned to predict the touch at the delay to which they were exposed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The extent to which participants unlearned to predict the immediate touch was significantly positively correlated with the extent to which participants learned to predict the delayed one.
source: Importantly, the extent to which participants unlearned to predict the immediate touch was significantly positively correlated with the extent to which participants learned to predict the delayed one (Pearson's r = 0.471, t(28) = 2.83, p=0.009, CI95 = [0.136, 0.712], BF10 = 6.150); Figure 2b), implying a temporal shift in the probability distribution of the tactile consequences in line with our hypothesized model (Figure 1a, middle and right).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There were no significant differences in the participants' discrimination ability (just noticeable difference) between conditions.
source: Finally, we noted that there were no significant differences in the participants' discrimination ability, that is just noticeable difference, between conditions (paired t-test between [0 ms, 0 ms] and [100 ms, 0 ms], t(29) = −0.76, p=0.452, CI95 = [−0.035, 0.016], BF10 = 0.254); paired t-test between [0 ms, 100 ms] and [100 ms, 100 ms], t(29) = 0.82, p=0.418, CI95 = [−0.018, 0.043], BF10 = 0.265)).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The absence of discrimination ability differences excludes response sensitivity differences between conditions as an alternative explanation.
source: This finding excludes the presence of response sensitivity differences between conditions as an alternative explanation of the present results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding about discrimination ability.

claim: The internal model generating the tactile predictions that produce somatosensory attenuation can be temporally retuned.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the internal model generating the tactile predictions that produce the somatosensory attenuation can be temporally retuned.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The attenuation of immediate touch decreased significantly as the number of exposure trials increased.
source: More specifically, the attenuation of immediate touch [100 ms, 0 ms] decreased significantly as the number of exposure trials increased (F(3,42) = 3.64, p=0.020), while the attenuation of delayed touch [100 ms, 100 ms] increased significantly as the number of exposure trials increased (F(3,42) = 4.86, p=0.005).
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The attenuation of delayed touch increased significantly as the number of exposure trials increased.
source: More specifically, the attenuation of immediate touch [100 ms, 0 ms] decreased significantly as the number of exposure trials increased (F(3,42) = 3.64, p=0.020), while the attenuation of delayed touch [100 ms, 100 ms] increased significantly as the number of exposure trials increased (F(3,42) = 4.86, p=0.005).
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 200 exposure trials compared to initial performance.
source: Replicating our previous results, the pairwise comparisons indicated a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 200 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.45, p=0.028, CI95 = [−0.168,–0.011], BF10 = 2.403) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [−0.198,–0.027], BF10 = 4.344) compared to the initial performance after 0 exposure trials, as well as a significant increase in the attenuation of the delayed touch after 50 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.98, p=0.010, CI95 = [0.019, 0.113], BF10 = 5.627), 200 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [0.022, 0.160], BF10 = 4.324) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = 3.38, p=0.004, CI95 = [0.034, 0.151], BF10 = 10.833) compared to the initial test.
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 500 exposure trials compared to initial performance.
source: Replicating our previous results, the pairwise comparisons indicated a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 200 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.45, p=0.028, CI95 = [−0.168,–0.011], BF10 = 2.403) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [−0.198,–0.027], BF10 = 4.344) compared to the initial performance after 0 exposure trials, as well as a significant increase in the attenuation of the delayed touch after 50 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.98, p=0.010, CI95 = [0.019, 0.113], BF10 = 5.627), 200 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [0.022, 0.160], BF10 = 4.324) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = 3.38, p=0.004, CI95 = [0.034, 0.151], BF10 = 10.833) compared to the initial test.
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in the attenuation of delayed touch after 50 exposure trials compared to initial test.
source: Replicating our previous results, the pairwise comparisons indicated a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 200 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.45, p=0.028, CI95 = [−0.168,–0.011], BF10 = 2.403) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [−0.198,–0.027], BF10 = 4.344) compared to the initial performance after 0 exposure trials, as well as a significant increase in the attenuation of the delayed touch after 50 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.98, p=0.010, CI95 = [0.019, 0.113], BF10 = 5.627), 200 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [0.022, 0.160], BF10 = 4.324) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = 3.38, p=0.004, CI95 = [0.034, 0.151], BF10 = 10.833) compared to the initial test.
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in the attenuation of delayed touch after 200 exposure trials compared to initial test.
source: Replicating our previous results, the pairwise comparisons indicated a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 200 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.45, p=0.028, CI95 = [−0.168,–0.011], BF10 = 2.403) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [−0.198,–0.027], BF10 = 4.344) compared to the initial performance after 0 exposure trials, as well as a significant increase in the attenuation of the delayed touch after 50 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.98, p=0.010, CI95 = [0.019, 0.113], BF10 = 5.627), 200 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [0.022, 0.160], BF10 = 4.324) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = 3.38, p=0.004, CI95 = [0.034, 0.151], BF10 = 10.833) compared to the initial test.
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in the attenuation of delayed touch after 500 exposure trials compared to initial test.
source: Replicating our previous results, the pairwise comparisons indicated a significant decrease in the attenuation of immediate touch after 200 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.45, p=0.028, CI95 = [−0.168,–0.011], BF10 = 2.403) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = −2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [−0.198,–0.027], BF10 = 4.344) compared to the initial performance after 0 exposure trials, as well as a significant increase in the attenuation of the delayed touch after 50 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.98, p=0.010, CI95 = [0.019, 0.113], BF10 = 5.627), 200 exposure trials (t(14) = 2.82, p=0.014, CI95 = [0.022, 0.160], BF10 = 4.324) and 500 exposure trials (t(14) = 3.38, p=0.004, CI95 = [0.034, 0.151], BF10 = 10.833) compared to the initial test.
evidence: This is a finding from the additional experiment supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The retuning of the internal model underlying somatosensory attenuation occurs through error-driven processes that evolve over time.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that the retuning of the internal model underlying somatosensory attenuation occurs through error-driven processes that evolve over time in response to repeated exposure to unexpected delays in the sensorimotor system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing trial-dependent effects.

claim: Somatosensory attenuation is considered one of the reasons for which we cannot tickle ourselves.
source: Somatosensory attenuation is considered one of the reasons for which we cannot tickle ourselves (Blakemore et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Self-tickling sensations are cancelled because the somatosensory feedback matches the tactile prediction of the internal model.
source: Accordingly, self-tickling sensations are cancelled because the somatosensory feedback of our movement matches the tactile prediction of the internal model and thus gets attenuated.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the internal model theory.

claim: Ticklish sensations arise from discrepancies (prediction errors) between the predicted feedback of the internal model and the actual somatosensory input.
source: In contrast, ticklish sensations arise from discrepancies (prediction errors) between the predicted feedback of the internal model and the actual somatosensory input (Blakemore et al., 2000a).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Participants rated their self-generated touch as more ticklish when a delay greater than 100 ms was introduced between the movement of one hand and the resulting touch on the other, compared to when a 0 ms delay was introduced.
source: An earlier study showed that participants rated their self-generated touch as more ticklish when a delay greater than 100 ms was introduced between the movement of one hand and the resulting touch on the other, compared to when a 0 ms delay was introduced.
evidence: This is a finding from previous literature, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: After exposure to the 0 ms delay, participants judged more frequently the delayed touch as being more ticklish than the immediate touch.
source: As expected from the literature, after exposure to the 0 ms delay participants judged more frequently the delayed touch as being more ticklish than the immediate touch (median frequency = 0.8, mean frequency = 0.73).
evidence: This is a finding from the tickling experiment supported by descriptive statistics.

claim: After exposure to the 150 ms delay, the frequency at which participants judged delayed touch as more ticklish significantly dropped.
source: Critically, after exposure to the 150 ms delay, this frequency significantly dropped (median frequency 0.6, mean frequency 0.65): Wilcoxon singed rank test, n = 30, V = 88, p=0.046, CI95 = [−0.2,–0.00002] (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the tickling experiment supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: After exposure to 150 ms delay, the delayed touch was rated significantly less frequently as the more ticklish one.
source: That is, the delayed touch was rated significantly less frequently as the more ticklish one, or, reversely, the immediate touch was rated significantly more frequently as the more ticklish one.
evidence: This is a restatement of the finding from the tickling experiment.

claim: After exposure to 150 ms delay, the immediate touch was rated significantly more frequently as the more ticklish one.
source: That is, the delayed touch was rated significantly less frequently as the more ticklish one, or, reversely, the immediate touch was rated significantly more frequently as the more ticklish one.
evidence: This is a restatement of the finding from the tickling experiment.

claim: Ticklishness sensations depend on the same learning mechanism that supports the attenuation of self-touch.
source: This result suggests that ticklishness sensations depend on the same learning mechanism that supports the attenuation of self-touch, thereby generalizing our findings beyond force intensity perception and suggesting a universal role of the sensory predictions –generated by a continuously retuned internal model– in the perceptual discrimination of self and non-self.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tickling experiment results.

claim: Sensory predictions generated by a continuously retuned internal model play a universal role in the perceptual discrimination of self and non-self.
source: This result suggests that ticklishness sensations depend on the same learning mechanism that supports the attenuation of self-touch, thereby generalizing our findings beyond force intensity perception and suggesting a universal role of the sensory predictions –generated by a continuously retuned internal model– in the perceptual discrimination of self and non-self.
evidence: This is a broader conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The present study investigated the temporal retuning of the internal model underlying the perceptual attenuation of self-generated touch.
source: The present study investigated the temporal retuning of the internal model underlying the perceptual attenuation of self-generated touch, the latter being a well-established index of the efference-copy-based sensory predictions (Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 2000a; Bays and Wolpert, 2008; Kilteni et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's objective.

claim: Perceptual attenuation of self-generated touch is a well-established index of efference-copy-based sensory predictions.
source: The present study investigated the temporal retuning of the internal model underlying the perceptual attenuation of self-generated touch, the latter being a well-established index of the efference-copy-based sensory predictions (Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 2000a; Bays and Wolpert, 2008; Kilteni et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the interpretation of somatosensory attenuation, supported by citations.

claim: The findings are strongly consistent with a gradual updating of the internal model during exposure to systematic delays.
source: Our findings are strongly consistent with a gradual updating of the internal model during exposure to systematic delays between the movement and the tactile feedback from the resulting self-touch (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in relation to the theoretical model shown in Figure 1a.

claim: After exposure to systematic delays, the delayed touch was predicted and thus attenuated.
source: After exposure to such delays, the delayed touch was predicted and thus attenuated, while the immediate (non-delayed) touch was not predicted and thus not attenuated.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: After exposure to systematic delays, the immediate (non-delayed) touch was not predicted and thus not attenuated.
source: After exposure to such delays, the delayed touch was predicted and thus attenuated, while the immediate (non-delayed) touch was not predicted and thus not attenuated.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The retuning of the internal model was driven by a prediction-error-based learning process.
source: Moreover, the magnitudes of these effects were correlated and dependent on the number of exposure trials, in line with our proposal that the retuning of the internal model was driven by a prediction-error-based learning process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation and trial-dependent findings.

claim: The dynamic retuning of the internal model influences the perceived ticklishness of tactile stimulation.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that this dynamic retuning of the internal model influences the perceived ticklishness of tactile stimulation, so that delayed touches feel less ticklish and non-delayed touches more ticklish after exposure to systematic delays.
evidence: This is a summary of the tickling experiment findings.

claim: The predictive learning process affects the perceptual quality of touch as being self- or externally generated beyond the mere intensity of the somatosensory feedback.
source: This demonstrates that the predictive learning process under discussion affects the perceptual quality of touch as being self- or externally generated beyond the mere intensity of the somatosensory feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tickling experiment results.

claim: The internal model underlying somatosensory attenuation during normal temporal conditions is dynamically retuned in presence of systematic delays.
source: We propose that the internal model underlying somatosensory attenuation during normal temporal conditions is dynamically retuned in presence of systematic delays, to encode the new temporal relationship between the motor command and the tactile consequence.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: The internal model is retuned to encode the new temporal relationship between the motor command and the tactile consequence.
source: We propose that the internal model underlying somatosensory attenuation during normal temporal conditions is dynamically retuned in presence of systematic delays, to encode the new temporal relationship between the motor command and the tactile consequence.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Exposure to delays could lead to the acquisition of a new internal model instead of adaptation of an existing one.
source: Rather than the adaptation of an existing internal model, it could be argued that the exposure to the delays leads to the acquisition of a new internal model instead.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis discussed by the authors.

claim: Witney et al. (1999) demonstrated significant grip force modulation after repeated exposure to systematic delay in a bimanual object manipulation task.
source: In a bimanual object manipulation task, Witney et al. (1999) demonstrated a significant grip force modulation after repeated exposure to a systematic delay between the movement of one hand and the resulting effects on the other hand, in a direction that is consistent with the acquisition of new internal model rather than the update of an existing one.
evidence: This is a finding from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: According to the new internal model hypothesis, the brain would learn different internal models for different delays and would switch between them.
source: According to this proposal, the brain would learn different internal models for the different delays and would switch between them (Wolpert and Kawato, 1998).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The data cannot differentiate between the hypothesis of updating an existing internal model and acquiring a new one.
source: Our data cannot differentiate between these two hypotheses since in both scenarios we would expect a decrease in the attenuation of the immediate touch and an increase in the attenuation of delayed touch.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the data.

claim: It is not known whether the same internal model underlies anticipatory grip force modulation during object manipulation and sensory attenuation during self-touch.
source: Moreover, it is not known whether the same internal model underlies the anticipatory grip force modulation during object manipulation and the sensory attenuation during self-touch.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: A shift in the predicted temporal distribution towards the newly predicted timing (update of an existing internal model) is more likely than the acquisition of a new one.

claim: A candidate brain area for the temporal retuning of the internal model could be the cerebellum.
source: We speculate that a candidate brain area could be the cerebellum, given its involvement in the implementation of the internal models (Wolpert et al., 1998), its well-established relationship with motor learning (Wolpert et al., 2011) and somatosensory attenuation (Blakemore et al., 1998b; Kilteni and Ehrsson, 2019) and its relevance to time perception and temporal coordination of movement according to evidence from nonhuman primates (Ashmore and Sommer, 2013), cerebellar patients (Ivry and Keele, 1989) and healthy subjects (Jueptner et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the cerebellum's known functions, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maintaining unbiased sensorimotor predictions is the root of motor learning.
source: Given that maintaining unbiased sensorimotor predictions is the root of motor learning (Shadmehr et al., 2010; Wolpert et al., 2011; Krakauer and Mazzoni, 2011), we propose that the observed effects are a new form of learning that represents the updating of the internal model's parameter specifying the temporal relationship between the motor command and its sensory feedback from the body.

claim: The present learning occurs in the temporal rather than the spatial domain.
source: In contrast to the classically studied motor (force-field and visuomotor) adaptation paradigms (Shadmehr et al., 2010; Krakauer and Mazzoni, 2011), the present learning occurs in the temporal rather than the spatial domain, and it serves to keep the sensorimotor predictions regarding one's own body (Kilteni and Ehrsson, 2017) temporally tuned.

claim: The observed temporal aftereffects mirror the classic spatial aftereffects observed in force-field and visuomotor adaptation.
